headline: Andy Burnham takes office, and rewires the state

body: Britain changed Prime Minister with its elected House on holiday. The Commons rose on Thursday 16 July for a recess that runs to 31 August; Sir Keir Starmer had taken his last Prime Minister’s Questions the day before, and the Speaker announced it from the Chair as “the final Prime Minister’s questions with the right hon. and learned Member for Holborn and St Pancras (Keir Starmer) as Prime Minister.” On Monday 20 July Andy Burnham became Prime Minister. On Tuesday 21 July a written statement, laid in the House of Lords in the name of the Lord Privy Seal and made on the Prime Minister’s behalf, informed Parliament that “Today, we are fundamentally rewiring the state, changing the geography of government.” Only one House was sitting to be told, and it was the unelected one.

The rewiring is not modest, and the only question put on it came from a peer. A new Office for the Prime Minister and the Cabinet, led by the Cabinet Secretary, will house No.10, the Cabinet Office teams serving the Prime Minister directly, and a new “No.10 North” built to run devolution and local growth. The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology is abolished outright: artificial-intelligence strategy and the AI Security Institute to the Cabinet Office, the digital brief to a strengthened Culture department, science and innovation to the Department for Business and Trade, renamed the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade. On the afternoon of 21 July Lord Clement-Jones put a Private Notice Question asking what that meant for the AI Safety Institute, the sovereign AI fund, the Government Digital Service and UK Research and Innovation. Baroness Anderson of Stoke-on-Trent, for the Cabinet Office, confirmed that UKRI and the sovereign fund go to the new business department, that UKRI’s £9.22 billion for research in 2026-27 continues, and that the Government Digital Service goes to Culture. Asked about the shape of the ministry itself, she said what a minister in a half-made Government must: “there are ongoing appointments in government, so I cannot possibly talk about any further roles and appointments that are being made, including my own.” Lord Waldegrave of North Hill, himself a former science minister, called it “the abolition and fragmentation of DSIT”; Lord Clement-Jones spoke of “the very regrettable resignation of the noble Lord, Lord Vallance,” and the Minister did not demur.

What the Commons did with its last two days was heavier than its two divisions suggest. On 15 July, without a division, it approved the first use of the designation power created by the state-threats Act that reached the statute book a week earlier. The draft National Security Act 2023 (Designated Bodies) Regulations 2026 designate the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the Islamic Movement of Companions of the Right and the GRU Volunteer Corps, making it an offence punishable by up to fourteen years to support, assist or take material benefit from any of them. “This debate is a significant moment,” Dame Angela Eagle told the House, “because this is the first use of a new power introduced by this Government.” The Opposition supported it and complained it had taken too long. It followed a general debate on Iran in which the Minister for Veterans and People, Calvin Bailey, told Members that Iranian forces had struck two UAE tankers in the strait of Hormuz, “killing an Indian crew member and injuring eight others,” and that the United Kingdom had “surged air power into the Gulf.” Four Acts received Royal Assent the same afternoon, and the King sent a Message inviting the Commons to consider the provision made for the financial support of the Sovereign. The week’s only divisions were deferred ones, taken on slips: a trade-union balloting order and its companion code of practice, each carried by 330 to 109.

Then, out of hours, the Government nationalised British Steel — and had to apologise for the manner of it. The Steel Industry (Nationalisation) Act had received Royal Assent on 15 July; the transfer into public ownership was executed “outside of working hours,” and the regulations were not laid before Parliament before they came into force. Facing an Urgent Question on the morning of 16 July from the Liberal Democrat Joshua Reynolds, the Under-Secretary Blair McDougall opened with “regret and apologies … that we were not able to lay the regulations before Parliament before they came into force.” The day before, Claire Coutinho had used an Urgent Question of her own to put whistleblower allegations about the National Energy System Operator’s control room to the Energy Minister, Michael Shanks, calling the investigation NESO has commissioned “a complete sham”; he replied that it was “irresponsible to suggest, in this place and on social media, that our energy system was at risk.” Both were repeated to the Lords on 20 July, after the Commons had gone. On the final morning Steve Reed announced the largest redrawing of English local government in a generation — 38 councils in place of 134 across the areas decided, nearly 3,000 fewer councillors, and a net saving that councils themselves project at about £1 billion by 2032-33 — and Stephen Doughty reported the UK-EU treaty on Gibraltar signed in Brussels on 14 July, with the last pieces of the frontier fence gone.

Beneath the Chamber, the written record ran hot and then kept running. In two sitting days 115 Members tabled 823 questions, and 2,216 answers were given across the eight days of this window — 1,226 of them after the House had risen. The paperwork has already caught up with the politics: four questions tabled on 15 and 16 July now stand on the record addressed to the Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, a department that did not exist when they were asked. Last week’s feature came back marked. All twelve of Rupert Lowe’s questions on RAF Barnham were answered on 15 and 16 July, each opening with the identical formula that the Government “is considering the use of MoD Barnham for asylum accommodation” and that “no final decision has been made”; two of them, as published, have the Government considering whether to “sue” MoD Barnham, and the answer on the cost of one day restoring the site is word for word the answer given about gym facilities and excursions. The graver seam was quieter: Josh Fenton-Glynn tabled five questions on drowning across three departments, one of them asking the Environment Secretary to discuss with the Prime Minister the appointment of a minister responsible for drowning prevention. And one Member spent his last two days building a file on the borough council in his constituency, which is this issue’s feature. The Commons does not sit again until September. The state it left behind on Thursday is not the state it will return to.

feature.title: The Basildon file: eighteen questions in two days
feature.department: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
feature.status: written questions tabled 15 – 16 Jul; all to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
feature.summary: On 15 July the Housing Secretary told the House, in a written statement on Best Value, that four new Best Value Notices had been issued, and that in the case of Basildon Borough Council his concerns related to “serious cultural and governance issues” — with an independent external assurance review commissioned to report by the end of October 2026. James McMurdock (Independent, South Basildon and East Thurrock) had two sitting days left. He used them to file eighteen questions on that single notice, eight on the day it was issued and ten on the last day before the rise. He asked what specific evidence led Ministers to conclude the notice was required; which Ministers and officials took the decision; on what date the Department first received the information that contributed to it; from which organisations, councillors and other individuals; what opportunities the council was given to respond; whether the review will examine procurement and contract management; what it will cost the public purse; whether its findings will be published in full; and whether concerns about the council’s readiness for local government reorganisation formed part of the decision. It is the written question used as a preservation order — not to change the outcome, which is already announced, but to fix the sequence of events in the record before six weeks of recess close over it.
questions: James McMurdock (Independent, South Basildon and East Thurrock) — eighteen questions on one Best Value Notice: the evidence base and the decision trail, who was consulted and who decided, the scope, cost and publication of the external assurance review, and the criteria by which the council will be judged to have improved.
The notice was announced the same day in the Housing Secretary’s written statement on Best Value, which also issued new notices to Hillingdon, Shropshire and Somerset, and lifted Dudley’s.
The cluster sits entirely with the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, and shadows the local government reorganisation statement made to the House twenty-four hours later.

qa.heading: RAF Barnham
qa.question: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, what estimate has been made of the total cost of returning MoD Barnham to its previous condition following the conclusion of its use as asylum accommodation; and which department will cover that cost.
qa.answer: The Government is considering whether to sue MoD Barnham for asylum accommodation. No final decision has been taken. If the site is taken forward, any activity provision, including where it would be delivered, would be considered as part of the operating model and ongoing suitability assessments.

qa.heading: Organs: Post-mortems
qa.question: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs, what steps her Department is taking to ensure that requests from the families of British nationals for the return of retained organs from overseas are progressed as quickly as possible through the relevant legal processes.
qa.answer: In any given year, the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office provides information and assistance in around 6,000 cases where a British person has died overseas. Every death is a personal tragedy, and our consular staff aim to provide practical, compassionate and timely support to those affected. We publish detailed country-specific guidance for Spain covering registering a death, the process of post-mortems and navigating local procedures. We work closely with Spanish authorities to help families navigate those processes. Where concerns are raised about systemic issues or significant delays affecting British families, we raise these with the relevant authorities and press them for improvements, including in Spain.

qa.heading: Schools: Temperature
qa.question: To ask the Secretary of State for Education, what steps her Department is taking to ensure that schools remain safe and operational during periods of extreme heat.
qa.answer: The department takes periods of hot weather and heatwaves seriously and has published a climate risk assessment. We continue to support responsible bodies and schools to provide education in a safe environment. To support them, the department has published guidance to support education settings during hot weather. This advice draws on guidance from the UK Health Security Agency. In most cases, schools are the safest place for children during hot weather, as staff can actively monitor pupils, ensure regular hydration, and make adjustments to keep them cool. Children may also not be any cooler at home than in school. Recent analysis by the National Housing Federation and the Chartered Institute of Housing shows that 1.6 million children are currently living in overheated homes.

votes.blurb: The week’s first division, and a deferred one — taken on slips rather than in the lobbies. The order, laid on 22 June, was approved 330 to 109.

votes.blurb: Its companion code of practice on electronic and workplace balloting, carried on the identical figures. The last two divisions before the rise.

bills.blurb: Royal Assent on 15 July, and used the same night. British Steel was transferred into public ownership before the regulations were laid, which cost the Government an apology at the Dispatch Box the next morning.
The year’s money, through both Houses on 14 July and given Royal Assent on 15 July with the Commons a day from rising.
The Hillsborough Law, carried through the Commons the week before, took its first reading in the Lords on 16 July. Second reading is set for 1 September.
Reached Lords report stage on 20 July, the day the new Prime Minister took office and four days after the Commons had gone home.
First reading in the Lords on 22 July — a reminder that one House was still legislating six days into the other’s recess.

intro: Britain changed Prime Minister with its elected House on holiday. The Commons rose on Thursday 16 July for a recess that runs to 31 August; Sir Keir Starmer had taken his last Prime Minister’s Questions the day before, announced as such from the Chair. On Monday 20 July Andy Burnham became Prime Minister. On Tuesday 21 July a written statement, laid in the House of Lords and made on the Prime Minister’s behalf, told Parliament that “Today, we are fundamentally rewiring the state, changing the geography of government” — abolishing the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, creating an Office for the Prime Minister and the Cabinet with a “No.10 North” inside it, and renaming the business department. The only question put on it was a Private Notice Question in the Lords. Behind it sat two crowded sitting days: the first use of the new state-threats designation power against the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a nationalisation of British Steel carried out outside working hours, which drew a ministerial apology, and 38 councils announced to replace 134.

overview.headline: Andy Burnham takes office and rewires the state
overview.intro: Britain changed Prime Minister while the House of Commons was in recess. The Commons rose on 16 July and does not sit again until September. Andy Burnham became Prime Minister on 20 July. On 21 July a written statement was laid in the House of Lords, on the Prime Minister's behalf, saying that the Government was fundamentally rewiring the state. The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology is abolished. Its work is split between the Cabinet Office, a strengthened Culture department and the Department for Business and Trade, which is renamed the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade. A new Office for the Prime Minister and the Cabinet is created, with a unit called No.10 North inside it to run devolution and local growth. Members of Parliament could not ask about any of it. The only question came from a peer in the House of Lords. The rest of the week belonged to the two sitting days before the rise.

brief.title: Prime Minister's Questions
brief.note: Sir Keir Starmer took his last session as Prime Minister. The Speaker told the House from the Chair that it was the final Prime Minister's Questions with him in office. Kemi Badenoch turned to what she called this Prime Minister's final questions and paid her own tribute to Ann Widdecombe. There has been no session since, because the Commons rose the next day.

brief.title: National security designations
brief.note: The Commons approved regulations designating the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the Islamic Movement of Companions of the Right and the GRU Volunteer Corps. Supporting or taking material benefit from a designated body now carries up to fourteen years in prison. Dame Angela Eagle told the House this was the first use of the new power. There was no division.

brief.title: British Steel
brief.note: The Steel Industry (Nationalisation) Act received Royal Assent on 15 July. The Government used it overnight to take British Steel into public ownership. The regulations were not laid before Parliament before they came into force. Answering an urgent question the next morning, the business minister Blair McDougall offered regret and apologies for that, and said the transfer had been done outside of working hours.

brief.title: Local government reorganisation
brief.note: Steve Reed announced decisions for the remaining two-tier areas of England. Across those areas 38 councils will replace 134. He told the House there would be nearly 3,000 fewer councillors, and that councils themselves project net savings of about £1 billion by 2032-33. Elections to the new councils are due in May 2027.

brief.title: Machinery of Government Changes
brief.note: A written statement laid in the House of Lords set out the new shape of government. A Private Notice Question from Lord Clement-Jones followed the same afternoon. Baroness Anderson of Stoke-on-Trent confirmed that UK Research and Innovation and the sovereign artificial intelligence fund move to the renamed business department, and that the £9.22 billion research budget for 2026-27 continues. Asked about her own position she said she could not talk about appointments still being made.

feature.title: The Basildon file
feature.summary: James McMurdock, the Independent Member of Parliament for South Basildon and East Thurrock, tabled eighteen written questions in two days on the Best Value Notice issued to Basildon Borough Council on 15 July. The Housing Secretary said his concerns there related to serious cultural and governance issues, and commissioned an independent review to report by the end of October 2026. McMurdock asked what evidence led Ministers to issue the notice, who was consulted, which Ministers and officials decided, what the review will cost and whether its findings will be published in full.
